title: Axilla, Cubital Fossa, Carpal Tunnel and Hand Spaces
introduction: Regional passageways of the upper limb—including the axilla, cubital fossa, carpal tunnel, and fascial spaces of the hand—conduct vital neurovascular bundles and flexor tendons across joints[cite: 101, 102, 111, 113]. Understanding their boundaries, contents, and communications is critical for safe clinical procedures like venipuncture and blood pressure measurement, as well as diagnosing nerve entrapments and deep hand infections[cite: 112, 119, 120, 127].
learningOutcomes: 3.1 Define the pyramid-shaped boundaries, walls, apex, base, and neurovascular contents of the axilla[cite: 102, 103, 104, 105, 106, 108].
3.2 Identify the boundaries, floor, roof, contents, and clinical applications of the cubital fossa[cite: 110, 111, 112].
3.3 Describe the attachments, relations, and contents of the flexor retinaculum and explain the pathophysiology of carpal tunnel syndrome[cite: 113, 114, 115, 116, 119].
3.4 Differentiate the fascial spaces of the hand (dorsal, midpalmar, thenar, web, and pulp spaces) and the forearm space of Parona[cite: 120, 122, 124, 125, 126, 127].
3.5 Distinguish common hand infections—including paronychia, felon, and deep fascial space infections—and explain their routes of spread and complications[cite: 130, 132, 134].

content.heading: The Axilla: Boundaries and Walls
content.body: The axilla is a pyramid-shaped space between the upper part of the arm and the side of the upper chest that provides passage for nerves, blood vessels, and lymphatics from the root of the neck to the upper limb[cite: 102]. It has an apex, a base, and four walls[cite: 102]. The apex is the cervicoaxillary canal, bounded by the 1st rib, clavicle, and superior edge of the scapula[cite: 102]. The base (axillary fossa or armpit) consists of concave skin, subcutaneous tissue, and axillary (deep) fascia extending from the arm to the thoracic wall around the 4th rib level, bounded by the anterior and posterior axillary folds, thoracic wall, and medial arm[cite: 103]. The anterior wall has two layers formed by pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, and the pectoral and clavicopectoral fascia, with pectoralis major and overlying skin forming the anterior axillary fold[cite: 104]. The posterior wall is formed by the scapula and subscapularis anteriorly, and by teres major and latissimus dorsi inferiorly; the posterior axillary fold (formed by latissimus dorsi, teres major, and skin) extends farther inferiorly than the anterior wall[cite: 105]. The medial wall consists of the thoracic wall (1st to 4th ribs and intercostal muscles) and overlying serratus anterior, while the lateral wall is a narrow bony wall formed by the intertubercular groove of the humerus[cite: 106].

content.heading: Contents of the Axilla and Posterior Wall Spaces
content.body: The axilla contains the axillary artery and its branches, the axillary vein and its tributaries, the infraclavicular part (cords and branches) of the brachial plexus, the intercostobrachial and long thoracic nerves, axillary lymph nodes (apical, central, lateral/humeral, pectoral, and subscapular groups), and loose areolar tissue and fat[cite: 107, 108]. The axillary neurovascular bundle is enclosed within a connective tissue sleeve called the axillary sheath[cite: 108]. Three key neurovascular openings are associated with the posterior axillary wall: the quadrangular space (transmitting the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery and vein), the triangular space (transmitting the circumflex scapular artery), and the triangular interval (transmitting the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery)[cite: 105].

content.heading: The Cubital Fossa: Boundaries, Contents, and Clinical Relevance
content.body: The cubital fossa is a shallow, triangular depression on the anterior surface of the elbow[cite: 110]. Its superior base is an imaginary line connecting the medial and lateral humeral epicondyles; it is bounded medially by the lateral border of pronator teres and laterally by the medial border of brachioradialis, with a floor formed by brachialis and supinator[cite: 110]. From lateral to medial, its four main vertical structures are the radial nerve (located between brachioradialis and brachialis in the vicinity of the fossa), the biceps brachii tendon, the brachial artery (which usually bifurcates near the inferior apex into the superficial radial artery and deeper ulnar artery), and the median nerve[cite: 111]. Superficial veins (median cubital, cephalic, and basilic veins) lie superficial to the fossa and are not part of its deep contents[cite: 112]. Clinically, the cubital fossa is used to auscultate the brachial artery during blood pressure measurement, palpate the brachial pulse, and obtain superficial venous access (phlebotomy)[cite: 112]. The bicipital aponeurosis forms the roof (ceiling) of the fossa and was historically termed the 'grace of God' tendon because it protected the underlying brachial artery and median nerve during venous blood-letting[cite: 112].

content.heading: Flexor Retinaculum and Carpal Tunnel Syndrome
content.body: The flexor retinaculum (also called the transverse carpal ligament or anterior annular ligament) is a strong fibrous band arching over the concavity of the carpus to form the carpal tunnel[cite: 113, 119]. It attaches medially to the pisiform and the hook of the hamate, and laterally to the tubercle of the scaphoid and the palmar ridge of the trapezium[cite: 114]. Superficially, it is continuous with the volar carpal ligament and palmar aponeurosis, and is crossed by the ulnar vessels and nerve along with the cutaneous branches of the median and ulnar nerves[cite: 115]. At its lateral end, the flexor carpi radialis tendon runs in a groove between its bony attachments; on its volar surface, palmaris longus and flexor carpi ulnaris partly insert, and the retinaculum gives origin to the short muscles of the thumb (thenar) and little finger (hypothenar)[cite: 116]. Packed inside the carpal tunnel are the long flexor tendons of the fingers (flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus) and thumb (flexor pollicis longus) together with the median nerve[cite: 113, 116, 119]. Any lesion narrowing the tunnel—such as an old fracture or arthritic change—compresses the median nerve, causing carpal tunnel syndrome (paraesthesiae, numbness, and motor weakness in the median nerve distribution)[cite: 119]. Because the superficial palmar cutaneous branch arises proximal to the retinaculum, sensation over the palm is usually spared; symptoms are relieved by dividing the retinaculum longitudinally[cite: 119].

content.heading: Fascial Spaces of the Hand and Space of Parona
content.body: The fascial compartments of the hand permit tendon mobility but offer little resistance to infection; they include the dorsal spaces (dorsal subcutaneous and dorsal subaponeurotic spaces), hypothenar space, midpalmar space, thenar space, web spaces, and pulp spaces[cite: 120, 122]. The intermediate palmar septum joins the palmar aponeurosis to the 3rd metacarpal bone, separating the midpalmar space from the thenar space[cite: 123, 124]. The thenar space lies on the thumb side of this septum, contains the first lumbrical muscle, is overlaid by the index finger flexor tendons, communicates proximally with the space of Parona, and communicates distally via lumbrical canals with the web spaces[cite: 124]. There are three web spaces surrounding the lumbrical tendons between the index, middle, ring, and little fingers that are continuous proximally with the palmar spaces[cite: 126]. The pulp spaces on the palmar fingertips and thumb contain fatty tissue subdivided by fibrous septa between the distal phalanx and skin; firm skin adherence at the distal flexion crease prevents proximal spread, while terminal digital vessels supplying the end of the distal phalanx (not the epiphysis) can be occluded by infection, causing bone necrosis[cite: 125]. In the distal forearm, the space of Parona extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm, roofed by flexor digitorum profundus tendons distally and flexor digitorum superficialis proximally, bounded by flexor carpi ulnaris medially and flexor pollicis longus laterally, with a floor formed by pronator quadratus distally and the interosseous membrane in its proximal two-thirds[cite: 127].

content.heading: Clinical Hand Infections
content.body: Paronychia is an infection of the lateral nail fold (paronychium), typically resulting from superficial trauma such as hangnails, nail biting, manicuring, finger sucking, or artificial nails[cite: 130]. A felon is an infection of the closed distal palmar phalanx compartment created by tangentially oriented fibrous septa, usually following penetrating trauma, hematogenous spread, or untreated paronychia[cite: 132]. Because the pulp space is closed, edema raises compartment pressure, impairing venous outflow and risking local compartment syndrome, myonecrosis, and osteomyelitis if bone is invaded[cite: 134]. Other serious hand infections include infectious tenosynovitis, herpetic whitlow, and deep fascial space infections involving the dorsal subaponeurotic space (located dorsal to the extensor tendons), subfascial web space, midpalmar space, and thenar space[cite: 134].

inTextQuestions.question: Which three bony structures bound the apex (cervicoaxillary canal) of the axilla?
inTextQuestions.answer: The 1st rib, the clavicle, and the superior edge of the scapula[cite: 102].

inTextQuestions.question: List the four main vertical structures associated with the cubital fossa from lateral to medial.
inTextQuestions.answer: Radial nerve (between brachioradialis and brachialis), biceps brachii tendon, brachial artery, and median nerve[cite: 111].

inTextQuestions.question: Why is palmar sensation usually spared in carpal tunnel syndrome?
inTextQuestions.answer: Because the superficial palmar cutaneous branch of the median nerve is given off proximal to the flexor retinaculum and does not pass through the carpal tunnel[cite: 119].

inTextQuestions.question: Which anatomical feature prevents a fingertip pulp space infection (felon) from spreading proximally along the finger?
inTextQuestions.answer: The firm adherence of the skin of the distal flexion crease to the underlying tissue, along with the compartmentalizing fibrous septa of the distal phalanx[cite: 125, 132].

saqs.question: Outline the structures forming the four walls (anterior, posterior, medial, and lateral) of the axilla.
saqs.answer: Anterior wall: pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, and pectoral/clavicopectoral fascia[cite: 104]. Posterior wall: scapula, subscapularis, teres major, and latissimus dorsi[cite: 105]. Medial wall: 1st to 4th ribs, intercostal muscles, and overlying serratus anterior[cite: 106]. Lateral wall: intertubercular groove of the humerus[cite: 106].

saqs.question: State the boundaries and floor of the cubital fossa, and explain why the bicipital aponeurosis was called the 'grace of God' tendon.
saqs.answer: The cubital fossa is bounded superiorly by a line connecting the humeral epicondyles, medially by the lateral border of pronator teres, and laterally by the medial border of brachioradialis, with a floor formed by brachialis and supinator[cite: 110]. The bicipital aponeurosis forms its roof and was called the 'grace of God' tendon because it protected the underlying brachial artery and median nerve during venous blood-letting[cite: 112].

saqs.question: Give the medial and lateral bony attachments of the flexor retinaculum and list the structures passing deep to it inside the carpal tunnel.
saqs.answer: Medially, the flexor retinaculum attaches to the pisiform and the hook of the hamate; laterally, it attaches to the tubercle of the scaphoid and the palmar ridge of the trapezium[cite: 114]. Deep to it inside the carpal tunnel pass the long flexor tendons of the fingers (flexor digitorum superficialis and profundus), the flexor pollicis longus tendon, and the median nerve[cite: 113, 116, 119].

saqs.question: Describe the boundaries of the space of Parona in the forearm.
saqs.answer: It extends from the proximal margin of the carpal tunnel to the mid-forearm, bounded proximally by the origin of flexor digitorum superficialis, medially by flexor carpi ulnaris, and laterally by flexor pollicis longus[cite: 127]. Its roof is formed distally by flexor digitorum profundus tendons and proximally by the belly of flexor digitorum superficialis, while its floor is formed by pronator quadratus distally and the interosseous membrane in its proximal two-thirds[cite: 127].

saqs.question: Differentiate between paronychia and a felon, and explain why an untreated felon can cause bone necrosis or osteomyelitis.
saqs.answer: Paronychia is an infection of the lateral nail fold (paronychium) caused by superficial nail trauma or artificial nails[cite: 130], whereas a felon is an infection of the closed distal palmar pulp space caused by penetrating trauma, hematogenous spread, or untreated paronychia[cite: 132]. Because fibrous septa divide the pulp space into closed compartments, infection increases pressure, impairs venous outflow, and can occlude terminal digital vessels supplying the end of the distal phalanx, leading to compartment syndrome, myonecrosis, bone necrosis, and osteomyelitis[cite: 125, 134].
